verses.zh: （大卫的诗，交与伶长。用丝弦的乐器，调用第八。）耶和华啊，求你不要在怒中责备我，也不要在烈怒中惩罚我！
verses.en: For the music director, to be accompanied by stringed instruments, according to the sheminith style;[NOTE:1] a psalm of David.Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.Do not discipline me in your raging fury.[NOTE:2]
notes: Psalm 6. The psalmist begs the Lord to withdraw his anger and spare his life. Having received a positive response to his prayer, the psalmist then confronts his enemies and describes how they retreat.
The meaning of the Hebrew term שְׁמִינִית (sheminit, “sheminith”) is uncertain; perhaps it refers to a particular style of music. See 1 Chr 15:21.
verses.commentary:
6:1 There are two IMPERFECTS used as JUSSIVES.

- rebuke – BDB 406, KB 410, Hiphil negated, cf. Ps. 38:1

- chasten – BDB 415, KB 418, Piel negated

This is a penitential psalm, as are Psalm 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, and 143.
The Jewish Study Bible (p. 1289) says that this Psalm of supplication has
become the liturgical weekday morning prayer of Jewish people.

▣ "in Your anger. . .in Your wrath"
The Psalm does not say why YHWH is angry (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN, I. C.). It may reflect the OT theology
of one causation. The psalmist had enemies, YHWH allowed/sent them (cf.
Ps. 6:3). Life's circumstances are

- punishment for sin (cf. Ps. 41:4)

- life in a fallen world (cf. Ps. 147:3)

- ways to strengthen faith (cf. 1 Cor. 10:13; Heb. 5:8)

However, one never knows which it is, so repent and have faith!

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

SPECIAL TOPIC: SUFFERING

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，求你可怜我，因为我软弱。耶和华啊，求你医治我，因为我的骨头发战。
verses.en: Have mercy on me,[NOTE:1] Lord, for I am frail.Heal me, Lord, for my bones are shaking.[NOTE:2]
notes: The implication is that the psalmist has sinned, causing God to discipline him by bringing a life-threatening illness upon him (see vv. 2-7).
Or “show me favor.”
verses.commentary:
6:2-3 Notice how "dismayed" (BDB 96, KB 111, Niphal PERFECT)
is related to both

- my bones (BDB 782), Ps. 6:2

- my soul (lit. nephesh, BDB 659, cf. Ps. 6:4), Ps. 6:3 (see full note at Ps. 3:2 and Gen. 35:18)

Both of these were ways of referring to a person's innermost life and
thoughts. This writer is in great distress and does not know why (i.e., like Job)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

6:2 As Ps. 6:1 asks YHWH for what not to do,
Ps. 6:2 asks YHWH to (also note Ps. 6:4)

- be gracious to me — BDB 335, KB 334, Qal IMPERATIVE

- heal me — BDB 950, KB 1272, Qal IMPERATIVE

The VERB "heal" does not necessarily
relate to a physical illness (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 1166, c, cf. Isa.
1:5-6), but to the attack of adversaries (cf. Ps. 6:7b, 10). However,
verse 2 leaves open the possibility of an illness. If an illness, why are
adversaries mentioned? Some would say the enemies made fun of the psalmist
(cf. Psalm 102:8) in his illness. The ancient Israelites believed sin and
sickness were related.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEALING

verses.zh: 我心也大大地惊惶。耶和华啊，你要到几时才救我呢？
verses.en: I am absolutely terrified,[NOTE:1] and you, Lord—how long will this continue?[NOTE:2]
notes: Normally the verb בָּהַל (bahal) refers to an emotional response and means “tremble with fear, be terrified” (see vv. 3, 10). Perhaps here the “bones” are viewed as the seat of the psalmist’s emotions. However, the verb may describe one of the effects of his physical ailment, perhaps a fever. In Ezek 7:27 the verb describes how the hands of the people will shake with fear when they experience the horrors of divine judgment.
Heb “my being is very terrified.” The suffixed form of נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh, “being”) is often equivalent to a pronoun in poetic texts.
verses.commentary:
6:3 "how long" This is the cry of
the human person made in God's image but trapped in a fallen mind, body,
and world (cf. Ps. 13:1; 74:10; 90:13)! As believers we must trust in God, not
circumstances, but still we cry out—why? When will it be over?

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，求你转回搭救我！因你的慈爱拯救我。
verses.en: Relent, Lord, rescue me![NOTE:1] Deliver me because of your faithfulness.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and you, Lord, how long?” The suffering psalmist speaks in broken syntax. He addresses God, but then simply cries out with a brief, but poignant, question: How long will this (= his suffering) continue?
Heb “my being,” or “my life.” The suffixed form of נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh, “being”) is often equivalent to a pronoun in poetic texts.
verses.commentary:
6:4 As Ps. 6:2 asks YHWH to act on the psalmist's behalf (i.e., "be gracious. . .heal"),
so too, Ps. 6:4.

- return – BDB 996, KB 1427, Qal IMPERATIVE

- rescue – BDB 322, KB 321, Piel IMPERATIVE

- save – BDB 446, KB 448, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

Notice the reason given for the requests is not the worth or merit of the
psalmist but the unchanging, merciful character of the covenant
creator/redeemer Deity!

One wonders what "return" in this context means. Did the
psalmist think YHWH had departed or hid Himself?

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

▣ "lovingkindness" This is the wonderful covenant NOUN!

SPECIAL TOPIC: LOVINGKINDNESS

verses.zh: 因为，在死地无人记念你，在阴间有谁称谢你？
verses.en: For no one remembers you in the realm of death.[NOTE:1] In Sheol who gives you thanks?[NOTE:2]
notes: Deliver me because of your faithfulness. Though the psalmist is experiencing divine discipline, he realizes that God has made a commitment to him in the past, so he appeals to God’s faithfulness in his request for help.

Heb “for there is not in death your remembrance.” The Hebrew noun זֵכֶר (zekher, “remembrance”) here refers to the name of the Lord as invoked in liturgy and praise. Cf. Pss 30:4; 97:12. “Death” here refers to the realm of death where the dead reside. See the reference to Sheol in the next line.
verses.commentary:
6:5 Psalm 6:5 gives the OT view of the
afterlife. Sheol was a place of consciousness but no joy or praise.
The whole issue of conscious existence beyond physical death is developed
through Scripture (i.e., Progressive Revelation). There are only hints in the OT (cf. Job 14:14-15;
19:25-27; Ps. 16:10; 49:15; 86:13; Isa. 25:8; 26:19; Ezek. 37:12-13; Dan.
12:1-2; Hos. 13:14). The full truth is revealed in 1 Corinthians 15!

The Hebrew Sheol (BDB 982) refers to the realm of the dead. It is characterized by

- a dark, gloomy place, Job 10:21-22; Ps. 143:3

- a place of no return, Job 10:21; 16:22

- a place of no praise to God, Ps. 6:5; 30:9; 8:10-12; 115:17 (silence, Ps. 94:17)

- a place separated from God, Ps. 88:5; 39:13, yet God is there, Ps. 139:8; Prov. 15:11!

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHERE ARE THE DEAD?, I. B.

Notice the author specifically mentions that in his understanding of Sheol, there is no

- remembrance (BDB 271)

- praise (BDB 392, KB 389, Hiphil IMPERFECT, cf. Ps. 30:9; 88:10-12; Isa. 38:18)

The Tyndale OT Commentary Series (vol. 15, p. 78) lists the imagery
used in the OT for Sheol.

- vast cavern – Ezek. 32:18-32

- stronghold – Ps. 9:13; 107:18; Matt. 16:18

- dark wasteland – Job 10:22

- a huge beast with a large mouth – Isa. 5:14; Jonah 2:2; Hab. 2:5

Thank God for a New Testament!

verses.zh: 我因唉哼而困乏；我每夜流泪，把床榻漂起，把褥子湿透。
verses.en: I am exhausted as I groan.All night long I drench my bed in tears;[NOTE:1] my tears saturate the cushion beneath me.[NOTE:2]
notes: The rhetorical question anticipates the answer, “no one.”sn In Sheol who gives you thanks? According to the OT, those who descend into the realm of death/Sheol are cut off from God’s mighty deeds and from the worshiping covenant community that experiences divine intervention (Pss 30:9; 88:10-12; Isa 38:18). In his effort to elicit a positive divine response, the psalmist reminds God that he will receive no praise or glory if he allows the psalmist to die. Dead men do not praise God!
Heb “I cause to swim through all the night my bed.”
verses.commentary:
6:6-7 The psalmist describes his physical
and emotional trauma caused by his "adversaries" (BDB 865, KB
1058, Qal PARTICIPLE, "those who
show hostility").

- weary with sighing (BDB 58)

- bed wet with tears (hyperbole)

verses.zh: 我因忧愁眼睛干瘪，又因我一切的敌人眼睛昏花。
verses.en: My eyes[NOTE:1] grow dim[NOTE:2] from suffering;they grow weak[NOTE:3] because of all my enemies.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “with my tears my bed I flood/melt.”
The Hebrew text has the singular “eye” here.
Or perhaps, “are swollen.”
Or perhaps, “grow old.”

verses.zh: 你们一切作孽的人，离开我吧！因为耶和华听了我哀哭的声音。
verses.en: Turn back from me, all you who behave wickedly,[NOTE:1] for the Lord has heard the sound of my weeping.[NOTE:2]
notes: In his weakened condition the psalmist is vulnerable to the taunts and threats of his enemies.
Heb “all [you] workers of wickedness.” See Ps 5:5.
verses.commentary:
6:8-10 The psalmist comes to a place of
mental relief as he trusted in YHWH, who has heard his prayer (cf. Ps.
28:6). This is expressed in three parallel lines (i.e., Ps. 6:8b, 9a, 9b).

Because of YHWH's acceptance of the prayer the adversaries

- must depart, Ps. 6:8a (cf. Ps. 119:115; 139:19)

- will be ashamed, Ps. 6:10 (cf. Ps. 71:13,24; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHAME)

- will be greatly dismayed, Ps. 6:10 (same VERB used of the psalmist in Ps. 6:2b and 3a)

- will turn back, Ps. 6:10 (same VERB used of YHWH in Ps. 6:4, but here
may be of going into Sheol, cf. Job 34:15; Ps. 9:18; Eccl. 3:20; 5:15; 12:7)

- will be suddenly ashamed (same VERB as Ps. 6:10a, cf. Ps. 73:19)

Numbers 2-5 are all IMPERFECTS used in a JUSSIVE sense.
The psalmist seeks the presence of YHWH but the absence of his foes! What they tried to do to him
is now done to them! This literary structure (i.e., reversal) is typical of the OT.
What humans expect is often opposite of what YHWH brings about (i.e., Isa. 55:8-11).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means
that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of
us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are
priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the
major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be
thought-provoking, not definitive.

- Describe Sheol from an OT perspective.

- Explain what "ashamed" means in an OT context.

- How does the anger and wrath of YHWH relate to the wicked and to the faithful follower?

verses.zh: 耶和华听了我的恳求；耶和华必收纳我的祷告。
verses.en: The Lord has heard my appeal for mercy;the Lord has accepted[NOTE:1] my prayer.
notes: The Lord has heard. The psalmist’s mood abruptly changes because the Lord responded positively to the lament and petition of vv. 1-7 and promised him deliverance.

verses.zh: 我的一切仇敌都必羞愧，大大惊惶；他们必要退后，忽然羞愧。
verses.en: They will be humiliated[NOTE:1] and absolutely terrified.[NOTE:2] All my enemies will turn back and be suddenly humiliated.
notes: The prefixed verbal form is probably a preterite here; it is parallel to a perfect and refers to the fact that the Lord has responded favorably to the psalmist’s request.

In the structure of the Psalm, this verse is either another petition or a statement of confidence. If a petition, the four prefixed verbal forms in this verse should be understood as jussives. By form, many prefixed verbs can be either imperfect or jussive. But the third verb in the series, יָשֻׁבוּ (yashuvu), can be distinguished as an imperfect by its qibbuts theme vowel, and is not a jussive (which would have had a qamets hatuph or holem). Expecting all four verbs to be the same due to parallelism leads to the conclusion that this section is a statement of confidence, in which the imperfect verbs should be treated as future.
